title: Cover-sheet memo
start: A single report about the size of a paperback lies squared on a pale neutral tabletop, a thick stack of ivory paper with crisp edges held by a brushed graphite binder clip. Its top sheet is plain where a cover sheet should be, and one small folded memo is clipped to its corner, the crease sharp. To the left, a graphite pneumatic tube terminal the height of a mug stands with its frosted acrylic canister docked. Behind the report sits an empty graphite in-tray, and to the right a small graphite pin rail holds a single blank card. The one acid-lime element is the tab of an unmarked cover sheet resting apart on the in-tray, the piece the report is actually missing. Faint paper dust lines the stack's edge.
end: The same report is almost gone under memos. Identical folded ivory memos burst from the mouth of the pneumatic terminal, which has spat its frosted canister onto its side, and a fan of memos is frozen mid-flight between the tube and the report. The in-tray has overflowed and slid forward, tipping a cascade of memos across the tabletop, and the pin rail sags with cards pinned three deep. Every memo lands on the report pile, clipped and overlapping, bowing the binder clip open. The lime cover-sheet tab is pinned flat beneath the drift at its left edge, barely showing. Creased corners, scuffed folds, a fine haze of paper fibre and a trail of memos lead straight back to the tube.
apocalypse: A wide miniature snowfield of layered ivory memos stretches to a pale horizon, its folds packed into ridges and crevasses like old glacier ice. Rising from it are the bleached tops of cubicle partitions in a long broken row, their graphite frames bent and half buried. In the foreground the pneumatic tube terminal, now the size of a silo, lies snapped at its base, its frosted canister cracked open and choked with fibre. Beyond it, a slim graphite gantry on four thin legs straddles a hollow where the original report lies exposed, its pages swollen and curled. The gantry's acid-lime clamping jaws are lowering one clean cover sheet squarely onto it, while a graphite survey stake marks the cleared hollow.

title: Exiled stapler
start: A heavy desk stapler about the length of a pencil rests on an ivory card blotter at the front of a pale neutral tabletop. Its upper arm is acid-lime enamel, the one lime element, over a brushed graphite base with a visible hinge pin. A crisp, pencil-thin graphite outline traced on the blotter marks its proper spot exactly. Behind it, a row of three miniature graphite desks recedes toward the back of the table, and on the right a narrow frosted acrylic stairwell model steps down out of frame. A folded ivory jacket hangs over the nearest desk chair, left by someone gone to lunch. Fine eraser crumbs and a few stray staples sit on the blotter, and dust softens the outline's edge.
end: The outline on the blotter is now empty, and the lime stapler has been pushed away across the whole layout. A skid trail of scuffed graphite marks and scattered staples runs from the outline past each desk, where boxes of papers have been dumped to fill its place. The stapler is frozen mid-tumble at the top of the frosted stairwell, tilted nose-down over the first step, its arm flipped open and a spray of loose staples hanging in the air below it. At the foot of the stairs, a dim graphite storage shelf is crammed with other displaced desk objects, a graphite tape dispenser and a frosted glass mug among them. The ivory jacket has slid off its chair onto the floor.
apocalypse: A flooded basement ruin spreads wide and low, still grey water reaching to a far row of cracked frosted-glass block pillars fading into haze. Islands of rubble break the surface: a toppled graphite storage shelf the size of a building, a sunken frosted mug, drifts of soggy ivory boxes slumping into the water. Snapped desk frames stand in lines like old piers. Near the centre, on a raised graphite landing, the old stapler sits weathered and pale, its paint worn back to bare metal. A slim graphite lift mast rises from the landing up through a broken slab toward a shaft of daylight, and its acid-lime platform has just cradled the stapler and begun to climb, water dripping from its underside.

title: Printer taken to the field
start: A compact desk printer about the size of a shoebox stands on a slim graphite cart with four small castors at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Its casing is matte graphite with chamfered corners and a frosted acrylic output tray. A single ivory sheet is jammed half out of the feed slot, crumpled into an accordion. The one acid-lime element is the small status lamp on the top panel, glowing to flag the jam. Behind the cart, a strip of pale ivory card runs to the back edge as a miniature pathway, and at the far right a patch of ivory paper grass, cut into thin fringed strips, marks an open field. Grey toner dust coats the tray lip, and the castors show faint scuffs.
end: The same cart has rolled along the ivory pathway and stopped at the edge of the paper-grass field, one castor snagged in the fringe and the cart pitching forward. The printer has slid off and landed on its side in the grass, lid sprung open, its frosted output tray snapped and lying a short span away. The jammed sheet has finally torn free and hangs frozen in the air above it, with a burst of loose ivory pages from the feeder fanning back toward the pathway. A cloud of grey toner dust hangs over the impact point, and small graphite screws and a roller spring lie scattered in an arc. The lime status lamp still glows from the upturned panel.
apocalypse: A wide overgrown meadow of ivory paper grass rolls toward low hills on the horizon, scorched grey in broad patches. Printer fragments lie scattered across it at building scale: a cracked graphite side panel standing upright like a wall, a split frosted tray bleached white, snapped rollers half sunk in the ground like fallen columns. Torn pages have weathered into pale sediment between the tufts. In the midground, a slim graphite rail sled runs on two thin tracks between a set of rebuilt feed rollers, and its acid-lime guide rollers are threading one clean sheet from a restored input tray through to a new frosted output tray, a single complete paper path running straight across the ruin.

title: Flair quota
start: An ivory paper lanyard strap about the length of a forearm hangs from a slim brushed graphite hook stand at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its clip resting on a blank ivory badge card. Three small round pin badges are fixed to the strap, each a plain graphite disc with a milled edge and no design. Beside the stand, a shallow frosted acrylic dish holds a supply of spare blank pins. The one acid-lime element is a thin marker on a graphite gauge bar at the stand's base, set at the minimum number of pins expected. To the left, a folded ivory card work shirt lies flat and crisp. Fine lint and a few loose pin backs rest on the tabletop.
end: The same lanyard strap is now fully armoured in pins, badges overlapping like scales from hook to clip. More have spread onto the folded ivory shirt, which has been dragged against the stand and sags under rows of graphite discs pinned into collar, cuffs and pocket, the card puckering around each one. The weight has bent the graphite hook into a curve, and the whole stand is tipping to the right, frozen mid-fall. The frosted dish has been knocked over, and a shower of pins is caught spilling across the tabletop, some bouncing, some rolling. The lime gauge marker is still visible at the base, but it has been pushed up to a higher notch. Scratches and pin backs litter the surface.
apocalypse: A wide grey shingle beach of loose graphite pin badges stretches to a flat horizon, countless discs layered in shallow terraces and wind-sorted by size. Half sunk in the shingle lie the ruins of the hook stand, now the height of a radio mast, bent double and flaking. Long strips of the ivory shirt are buried in ridges, pierced and frayed, bleached almost white. Pin backs collect in small drifts in the hollows. In the midground, a slim graphite crane on a tracked base swings its boom over the shingle, its acid-lime electromagnet plate lowered just above the surface as a cluster of pins leaps upward to meet it. Beneath the boom sits one small frosted acrylic tray holding a neat single layer of pins.

title: Insomnia copier
start: A desktop copier about the size of a small suitcase sits at the left of a pale neutral tabletop, matte graphite with chamfered edges, its sandblasted frosted glass lid slightly raised over the original. A single crisp ivory copy lies in the frosted acrylic output tray, sharp-edged, its blank layout of blocks and ruled lines matching the original exactly. The one acid-lime element is the copier's round start key on the top panel. To the right, an empty graphite in-tray waits, and a cold frosted glass mug with a dried ring sits near the table edge, left from a long evening. Faint toner dust shows along the tray lip. Soft grey light suggests the very small hours of the night.
end: The same copier is running flat out. Its lid is propped open with a copy on the glass instead of the original, and each copy feeds out a little greyer and grainier than the last, the blocks and lines smudging into mottled speckle. Copies stream from the tray in a continuous arc, frozen mid-air, landing in a sliding stack that has overflowed the in-tray and spread across the tabletop toward the mug, which is tipping over the edge. The lime start key is held down under a wedged graphite ruler. The original ivory sheet lies trapped beneath the pile with one corner showing. A warm toner haze drifts above the copier, and fine grey powder coats everything downstream.
apocalypse: A wide dune sea of grey copies rolls away under dim night light to a flat horizon, each dune built from countless faded, grainy sheets packed into drifts, their surfaces rippled by wind. Near the foreground the copier rises from a dune, now the size of a warehouse, its frosted lid snapped off, its glass cracked and silted with toner. The fallen mug lies rim-up in a hollow, filled with grey powder. In the midground, a slim graphite scanning bridge on two thin legs spans a trough between dunes, its acid-lime light bar sweeping slowly along the sheets below. At the bridge's end, a jointed graphite arm lifts one crisp, bright ivory original clear of the grey drift.

title: Clock-tower deadline
start: A slender office tower model about the height of a wine bottle stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Its body is matte graphite with fine machined window grooves on every floor, each window a small panel of frosted acrylic glowing softly. Near the top, a round clock dial of sandblasted frosted glass over an ivory dial with plain tick marks fills one side. Its graphite hour pointer sits near the top, and a single acid-lime minute pointer is a few ticks away from meeting it. At the tower's base lies a tidy ivory card forecourt with a small stack of blank folders. Light dust gathers in the window grooves. Everything is still and correct.
end: The same tower, with the acid-lime minute pointer frozen one tick from the top. The floors below have filled with unfinished work: ivory sheets press against every frosted window, several panes have popped out, and sheets pour from them in streams down the facade. A cascade from the upper floors is caught mid-fall, sheets fluttering outward, and on the forecourt the folder stack has been buried under a growing drift that spreads toward the table edge. The lowest floor has bulged, its window frame split and a jammed wedge of folders forcing it open. Paper dust hangs in the air around the clock. Every stream can be traced from the clock down the facade to the pile.
apocalypse: A high, snowy mountain ridge of compacted ivory paper stretches along a wide horizon under a cold pale sky. Along it stand the stumps of old graphite towers, and the tallest is the clock tower, now the size of a peak, cracked down its facade with its frosted windows long gone and packed with snow-like paper. Its clock dial is split, both pointers hanging loose. Glaciers of old sheets flow down from the empty windows into the valley below. On a ledge beside the clock, a slim graphite winch rig bolted to the stonework feeds a lime drive gear into the exposed mechanism, and the gear has just engaged: the loose minute pointer has lifted and moved one tick.

title: Late-night book delivery
start: A bound mock-up book about the size of a thick hardback sits on the bottom step of a townhouse staircase model on a pale neutral tabletop. It has plain ivory card covers, a blank spine and a stitched block of crisp pages, and the one acid-lime element is a single ribbon bookmark hanging from its lower edge. The staircase is ivory card treads on graphite stringers, rising to a closed graphite front door with a frosted glass fanlight glowing faintly above it. Beside the book, a graphite key and a folded coat lie on the step. The scene is lit as late night, a soft glow on the treads. Fine dust and a scuffed corner show on the book.
end: The same staircase has stretched. New ivory card treads have been added again and again, so the stairs now climb far higher and steeper, bending toward the back of the tabletop, the frosted fanlight a small glow at the very top. The book has grown heavier: extra ivory sections are being bound into it, loose pages frozen mid-air as they fly in and slot between the covers, and the spine is splitting. Its weight has cracked the bottom tread, which sags, and the book is sliding off it, tipping backward. The lime ribbon bookmark trails straight up the stairs toward the door. The key is falling through the crack, and dust puffs from the broken tread.
apocalypse: A quiet night street of weathered ivory townhouses stretches away along a hillside, windows dark, toward a faint glow on the horizon. In the foreground, the long staircase has collapsed into a slope of snapped treads and bent graphite stringers, like scree climbing to a doorway far above. The book lies at the bottom, now the size of a house, its covers warped and its swollen pages fanned and bleached, loose sections drifted across the street like fallen leaves. A slim graphite funicular rig has laid a pair of straight rails up the ruined slope, and its acid-lime carriage cradle carries the book halfway up on a levelled platform, toward the graphite front door where the frosted fanlight still glows.

title: Coffee-run relay
start: A four-slot carrier tray of moulded ivory card, about the width of a paperback, sits at the front left of a pale neutral tabletop. One slot holds a tall ivory paper cup with a frosted acrylic lid, and a thin curl of steam rises from its sip hole. A crisp acid-lime paper sleeve wraps that cup, marking the one order that matters. The other three slots are empty, their pressed fibre walls showing faint mould seams. To the right, a brushed graphite pickup shelf holds a blank ivory order slip under a small graphite bulldog clip. Behind it, a short stack of unused trays waits, nested neatly. A few loose fibres and one faint ring of condensation mark the tabletop. Everything is square, still and on time.
end: The same carrier tray is now the base of a leaning tower of nested trays a dozen high, every slot filled with an ivory cup, the frosted lids fogged and no steam left anywhere. The tower sways to the right, frozen mid-lean. The top two trays are sliding free and three cups are tipping out, lids popping off and pale milky coffee arcing through the air in thick droplets. The original cup with the acid-lime sleeve is trapped at the very bottom, slightly crushed, its sleeve creased. Blank order slips have piled on the graphite pickup shelf until it bows in the middle. Spilled milky liquid runs across the tabletop toward the front edge, soaking the tray bottoms dark and soft. Cold condensation beads on every cup.
apocalypse: A wide, flat delta of dried pale milky sediment spreads to a low horizon, cut by shallow braided channels that still hold thin films of liquid. At its head stands the collapsed tower of carrier trays, now the size of a tenement block, its ivory card walls bleached, sagging and split along the moulded seams. Toppled cups the height of grain silos lie half sunk in the silt, their frosted lids cracked and scattered like fallen roof domes. The graphite pickup shelf juts from a channel bank as a pitted, bowed pier. In the foreground, a slim graphite cable crane on three splayed legs lowers an acid-lime cradle around one intact cup and lifts it clear of the mud. Fine dust lines every ridge, and tide rings circle the ruins.

title: Autopilot remote
start: A slim handheld remote, about the length of a pencil, lies diagonally at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Its body is brushed graphite metal with chamfered edges, two small screws on the back plate and a grid of blank frosted acrylic buttons. One oval button near the top is acid-lime, slightly worn at its centre from use. To its left stands a tear-off desk calendar on a graphite easel base: a thick block of blank ivory paper pages bound under a graphite clip. Behind the calendar sit a cold frosted glass mug and a folded ivory card note, left by someone who stepped out. Only the top calendar page lifts slightly, curling at one corner. Light dust rests along the remote's seams.
end: The same remote now lies with its acid-lime button pressed flat, held down by the folded card note, which has slipped onto it. The tear-off calendar is shedding pages in a continuous stream: dozens of blank ivory sheets are frozen mid-air, fanning out to the left in a long arc like a riffled deck, the nearest sharp and the farthest smeared with motion. The calendar block has shrunk to a thin sliver under its clip. The desk around it has aged in the same moment. The frosted mug is clouded with a ring of dried residue, the tabletop is furred with dust, and the pages already lying at the edge are yellowed and brittle, curling at the corners. The paper stream traces straight back to the clip.
apocalypse: A grey-ivory basin of drifted paper stretches away under still, dusty air, the drifts layered like old snow and the lowest sheets pressed into brittle beige strata. Near the middle rises the calendar easel, now the size of a radio mast, its graphite clip jaws open and empty, one leg buckled. The remote lies half buried nearby like a fallen bridge span, its frosted buttons clouded and cracked, the back plate lifted at one corner around a stripped screw. A frosted glass mug as big as a water tower sits tilted and filled with dust. In the foreground, a low graphite tracked rig extends a long boom and presses an acid-lime pad onto the remote's worn pause button, and the nearest drift has stopped creeping, its leading edge frozen.

title: Say yes to everything
start: A shallow inbox tray of brushed graphite, about the size of a letter sheet, sits front centre on a pale neutral tabletop, holding one ivory request slip with a neatly folded corner. To its right stands a spring-loaded desk stamp: a graphite handle, a chamfered column and a square rubber front inked in acid-lime, poised above an empty blotter of ivory card. The spring is visible through a frosted acrylic sleeve on the column. Behind them sits a graphite outbox tray, still empty and waiting. A cold frosted mug sits at the back right corner. Fine fibres lift from the slip's deckled edge, and a thin film of dust rests on the blotter. The desk is tidy, and the flow is one slip in, one slip out.
end: The same stamp is frozen at the bottom of a hard stroke, its spring fully compressed, and every slip in reach now carries its acid-lime ink square. Slips pour out of the inbox tray, which has overflowed into a heap, and a blizzard of stamped ivory slips is frozen mid-air, arcing up and to the right over the outbox tray, now buried in a drift. Some slips carry two or three overlapping squares. The ivory blotter is soaked through with ink and curling at its corners. A fan of slips has slid off the far edge of the table, and a few have landed across the cold mug. A trail of tiny ink droplets and bent slip corners runs straight back to the stamp front.
apocalypse: A frozen avalanche of ivory slips has swept down a long valley, burying a grid of low graphite blocks that read as a city seen from far above; only rooftops and a few chamfered towers break the surface. Every slip is faded, the old ink squares bleached to a dull pale grey. At the head of the valley the stamp lies on its side, now as big as a cathedral, its spring snapped and uncoiled across the paper snow, its handle cracked through. Across the valley mouth stands a slim graphite sorting gate on stilts with an acid-lime sieve screen. The slips pile against it, and only a thin trickle passes through into a neat graphite channel below, stacking into a short, orderly pile. Dust hangs in the valley air.

title: Door vault conveyor
start: A tall graphite storage rack, about the height of a wine bottle, stands at the right of a pale neutral tabletop, divided into narrow vertical slots like a plate rack. A thin graphite floor rail runs from the left edge into its base. Six slots hold miniature plain doors: flat ivory card panels with bevelled edges and small graphite knobs, each in a slim graphite frame. On the rail, one more framed door is sliding into the next empty slot, a tiny acid-lime latch on its frame about to click home. Two slots remain empty. A few card fibres and a fine line of metal dust sit in the rail's groove. The rack is plumb and evenly spaced.
end: The same rack is being overfed. Framed doors crowd the floor rail nose to tail, pushed in faster than the rack can take them. The door with the acid-lime latch has missed its slot and wedged diagonally across two, its frame bent. Behind it the rail has buckled upward, and a pile-up of doors is frozen mid-collision: several have swung open in their frames, two knobs have popped loose and hang airborne, and one door is falling off the rail toward the viewer. Inside the rack, doors have been shoved sideways and lean against each other like toppled dominoes. Card panels crease at their hinges, and bright metal shavings glint along the buckle, all tracing back to the jammed slot.
apocalypse: A broad canyon floor runs between two sheer walls built from stacked, bleached ivory door panels, layered like sedimentary rock. Scattered across the floor are fallen door frames the size of barns, some standing on edge, others lying flat and half filled with drifted card fibre, their loose knobs resting like boulders. The storage rack closes the canyon's far end, its graphite uprights rising as broken, leaning pylons, the slots empty or jammed with shattered panels. The old floor rail runs through the drift as a buckled, pitted line. In the midground, a slim graphite gantry crane on paired rails lifts one intact door and lowers it into a rebuilt section of rack, where acid-lime alignment arms clamp the frame square. Dust haze fills the canyon.

title: Production line escape
start: A compact production line of brushed graphite stretches left to right across a pale neutral tabletop, about the length of a ruler. Small ivory card cartons, crisply folded with blank labels, ride a matte belt in even spacing from a stamping press at the left toward a single square hatch at the right end, cut into a frosted acrylic wall. The hatch has a sliding graphite shutter, raised just a finger's width, with an acid-lime pull handle. A graphite crank sits idle beside the press. Behind the line, a folded ivory card apron hangs from a peg, left by whoever runs the shift. Fine card dust coats the rollers, and faint scuffs mark the belt's edges.
end: The same line has sped up: the belt is a blur, and the press at the left is kicking out cartons far faster than the hatch can pass them. At the right end the cartons have jammed against the barely open shutter, crumpling and stacking into a leaning wall that has shoved the frosted acrylic panel out of true. Behind the jam, cartons back up along the whole belt, riding over each other, and several are frozen mid-air where they have popped off the sides. The acid-lime pull handle is pinned under a crushed carton, out of reach. The crank spins loose on its axle, the apron has fallen from its peg, and flattened cartons slide off the table toward the viewer. Card dust hangs over the jam.
apocalypse: A long, collapsed factory ruin lies in a shallow valley at dawn, low light raking across it. The production line has become a long embankment of fused, crushed cartons, their ivory card grey and layered like shale, with graphite rollers poking out like broken pipes. The stamping press stands at the far end as a toppled tower, its ram snapped. The frosted acrylic wall at the near end is cracked and leaning, and beyond it opens a wide meadow of pale ivory grasses rolling to the horizon. In the foreground, a slim graphite winch rig anchored on splayed legs hauls the old hatch shutter, now tall as a barn door, upward on an acid-lime cable, while a narrow graphite ramp is being laid through the gap into the field.

title: Cold-call phone bank
start: A single desk telephone, about the size of a paperback, sits on a bare graphite desk at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, with wide empty space around it suggesting a large open floor. The phone has a matte graphite body, a frosted acrylic keypad with blank keys and a handset resting in its cradle on a neat coiled cord. A small acid-lime indicator lamp on its front is lit, marking one incoming line. Beside it lies an ivory card call sheet with blank ruled lines and a graphite pen. An empty graphite chair is pushed back from the desk, a folded ivory card jacket draped over it. Fine dust sits in the keypad grooves, and the cord shows slight wear.
end: The same desk is now one of many. Phones have multiplied across the tabletop into a crowded trading floor: handsets on every surface, stacked two and three high on desks, piled on chairs, lined up along the floor between them. Every handset has jolted out of its cradle and hangs frozen a finger's width above it, cords stretched. Call sheets have slid off the desks in drifts. The original phone at the centre is buried under a heap of others, only its acid-lime lamp still glowing through the pile. The empty chair has rolled backward and tipped, its jacket sliding off. Rattling handsets have walked across the desks, leaving scuffs, and dust shakes loose in fine clouds.
apocalypse: A vast, silent flatland of dead handsets stretches to a hazy horizon, each one the size of a car, bleached and cracked, receivers lying off their cradles and half sunk in a floor of drifted, yellowed call sheets. Coiled cords as thick as tree trunks lie slack and snapped between them. Frosted keypads lie scattered like broken tiles. In the middle distance, the original desk rises as a weathered platform on bent graphite legs, its phone a slumped mound. Nothing is ringing. In the foreground, a slim graphite line-laying rig on a narrow wheeled chassis unspools a single acid-lime cable across the plain, running from one handset it has lifted and set upright back to the old desk.

title: Pudding loophole
start: A single dessert cup, about the size of a shot glass, stands on a brushed graphite stockroom shelf that runs across the back of a pale neutral tabletop. The cup is frosted acrylic with a milky glow, sealed with a crisp ivory paper lid pressed flat at the rim. Beside it, clipped to the shelf edge by a small graphite clip, hangs one coupon of ivory card with deckled perforated edges, a blank front and a thin acid-lime stripe along its top border. The rest of the shelf is empty. Below, a folded ivory delivery slip and a graphite box cutter lie on the tabletop. Fine dust sits along the shelf lip.
end: The same shelf now sags under towers of identical frosted cups, stacked in pyramids and columns up to the top of the frame. The shelf has bowed in the middle, and cups slide off it in a frozen cascade, rolling across the tabletop in a flood that pours toward the front edge, out toward unseen warehouse aisles. The coupon hangs at a steep angle from its clip, its acid-lime stripe still visible, and a long ribbon of plain clipped coupons now trails from it down to the floor. Delivery slips have piled into a drift, and several paper lids have popped off and hang mid-air. The box cutter is buried under the cups.
apocalypse: A vast warehouse ruin opens under a broken graphite roof, pale sky showing through the gaps. Its floor has become dunes of frosted cups, each now the size of a car, drifted in rippling banks against toppled racking, lids peeled and bleached, some cracked and filled with pale grit. The old aisles show as troughs between the dunes, running to a hazy back wall. The stockroom shelf juts out of the nearest dune as a bent girder, its faded coupon still clipped on. In the foreground, a low, slim graphite pallet rig with acid-lime forks pulls out from under a dune, carrying one tidy pallet of cups stacked square and strapped with ivory card bands along a cleared lane toward an open loading door.

title: Auto-layoff machine
start: A row of five small office desks, each about the size of a matchbox, lines up across a pale neutral tabletop on a pair of slim graphite rails set flush into the surface. Each desk is brushed graphite with an ivory card top, a tidy stack of ivory papers and a pushed-in chair. On each desk sits a slim graphite evaluation box the size of a sugar cube, with a frosted acrylic window and a small flag arm folded down. Only the box on the middle desk has its acid-lime flag arm lifted, halfway up. At the right end of the rails, a short graphite ramp slopes down to the table edge. Fine dust lies in the rail grooves.
end: The same row is mid-ejection. The evaluation boxes are flagging desks automatically, flag arms rising one after another, and flagged desks are frozen shooting sideways along the rails, papers lifting off their tops in sheets, chairs tipping backward off them. The middle desk with the acid-lime flag leads the way, already launched off the ramp and caught in mid-air past the table edge, its box still attached. Two more desks follow close behind, grinding on the rails in bursts of metal dust. Gaps open in the row where desks stood, and the remaining boxes are just raising their plain graphite flags. Papers drift in a trail back along the rails.
apocalypse: A wide plain of dry ivory grass spreads under a pale horizon, scattered with ejected desks the size of houses lying where they landed: upturned, sunk on one corner, split open with papers spilling into the grass. Deep gouges run from each desk back toward the centre, where a burnt-out evaluation box, now the size of a control bunker, sits scorched dull grey, its frosted window cracked and its flag arms seized. The old rails radiate outward, bent and broken. In the midground, a slim graphite rail-laying rig with acid-lime tongs has placed one fresh straight pair of rails and is setting a single desk back onto them, square and level, the start of a restored row.

title: Concession overflow
start: A cinema concession counter of brushed graphite metal runs across the midground of a pale neutral tabletop, about a forearm long, with a chamfered front edge. On its left end stands a popcorn cabinet the size of a shoebox: sandblasted frosted-glass walls, a graphite roof and a small graphite kettle hung inside. The kettle's acid-lime lid tips gently open, releasing the first few puffs. A shallow layer of popcorn made from crumpled ivory paper nuggets covers the cabinet floor. On the right sit three empty ivory card cartons, crisply folded and unmarked, and a graphite scoop hangs on a hook. A folded ivory apron rests on the counter, left behind at the end of a shift. Paper crumbs dot the counter, and a faint haze clings to the frosted glass.
end: The same counter under an overflowing kettle. Its acid-lime lid is flipped fully back and ivory paper popcorn erupts in a thick column, packing the frosted cabinet solid and bursting its front door open. Popcorn cascades along the counter in a drift that has swallowed the three cartons, tipping one onto its side. The graphite scoop has been knocked off its hook and is caught mid-fall off the front edge, trailing kernels. The folded apron is being carried toward the right end on a rolling wave of puffs. Loose pieces hang in the air above the kettle, a pale dust rises from the drift, and every ripple in the pile slopes back to the cabinet on the left.
apocalypse: A wide field of pale ivory popcorn dunes, crumpled paper puffs weathered grey at their crests, rolls away to a low horizon. Half buried in the nearest dune is a giant graphite counter, its front edge snapped and its surface cracked. Behind it the frosted cabinet has collapsed into shards the size of doors, their milky edges poking from the drifts, and the kettle lies on its side like a toppled bell. A graphite scoop the size of a boat is wedged upright in the middle distance. Across the foreground, a slim graphite plough rig on narrow caterpillar tracks pushes its lime blade forward, carving one clean, level path through the dunes back toward the counter, the cleared floor behind it smooth, pale and swept.

title: Cloned yourself
start: One tidy workstation sits on a pale neutral tabletop: a graphite desk the size of a shoebox with crisp chamfered edges, a graphite chair tucked squarely under it, and a single frosted acrylic mug with a faint ring of dried coffee inside. At the desk's right corner sits a small graphite photocopier the size of a matchbox, its sandblasted frosted-glass bed lit from beneath. Its acid-lime copy button glows, pressed once. A neat ivory notepad lies squared beside the mug, and a folded ivory cardigan hangs over the chair back. The desk's machined surface shows fine concentric marks, and light dust sits in the copier's seams. Everything is single, straight and freshly set, one of each.
end: The same desk, copied again and again. From the original in the foreground, a row of desks marches off to the right, each a slightly worse copy: the second soft at its edges, the third warped and pale, the fourth made of crumpled ivory card, the last a flimsy folded sheet collapsing under its own mug. The acid-lime copy button on the original copier is stuck down, and a fresh desk is sliding out of its side. Mugs tip and spill thin grey streaks, chairs lean further with each copy, and cardigans fray into loose fibres. A drift of misprinted ivory sheets flies up between the copies, all tracing back to the copier at the head of the line.
apocalypse: A long, flat plain stretches to a vanishing point, lined with a receding avenue of ruined desks, each more eroded than the last until the far ones are only mounds of grey paper pulp. Near the viewer, the original graphite desk stands the size of a house, weathered and scuffed but whole, its copier toppled on the ground beside it with the frosted bed cracked. Bleached mugs lie scattered like boulders, and fallen chairs splay across the plain. Drifts of misprinted sheets fill the gaps. In the midground, a slim graphite crane on a single track lowers a lime rectangular frame over the original desk, fixing it in place, while a small graphite sweeper beside it begins pushing the nearest copies into neat bales.

title: Systems are down
start: A curved control console of brushed graphite metal, about a forearm wide, sits at the front of a pale neutral tabletop. Its angled deck holds rows of small frosted acrylic toggle keys, each softly lit from within, and three blank frosted-glass panels glowing evenly. One small acid-lime warning lamp at the far right blinks, the only fault. Behind the console, a narrow corridor model runs back into the midground, lined with four graphite security doors, all shut, their seams tight. An empty graphite swivel chair is turned toward the deck, with a frosted mug and a crumpled ivory paper sandwich wrapper beside it. Fine dust lies in the gaps between keys, and the doors show faint machining marks.
end: The same console going dark. From the acid-lime warning lamp at the right, the fault spreads leftward: the frosted keys switch off in a rippling line, two of the three panels have gone dull grey and the third flickers. Down the corridor behind, the graphite security doors slide open in sequence, the first fully open, the second halfway, the third just cracked and the fourth still shut, each one tripped by the last. The swivel chair has spun and rolled into the corridor mouth. The mug is tipped, a thin grey spill running into the key gaps. A drift of ivory paper printouts pours from a slot under the console, caught mid-fall, and dust sifts down from the open door frames.
apocalypse: A wide, overgrown ruin spreads toward a misty horizon, thick with fronds and vines cut from ivory paper, curling and yellowed at their tips. The giant graphite console lies tilted in the foreground, its frosted panels cracked and furred with paper moss, keys missing like lost teeth. Beyond it, the corridor has become a long canyon of graphite doors, each as tall as a tower and stuck at a different gap, with paper vines pouring through them. Drifts of old printouts lie matted into the ground. In the midground, a slim graphite cable-laying rig on thin jointed legs threads a line across the canyon floor and pushes a single lime master switch into the console's base, and the first row of frosted keys nearest it glows again.

title: Sinking launch
start: A tabletop sea of frosted acrylic waves, rippled and softly glowing from within, fills a shallow graphite tray about a forearm long. Riding at its centre is a flat product-launch barge the size of a shoebox, its hull brushed graphite metal with a chamfered bow and neat rivet rows. On its deck sits a single product crate of ivory card, crisply folded and tied with graphite wire. Along the barge's rail hang four small ivory paper lifeboats on graphite davits, and one acid-lime lifebuoy is clipped at the stern. A folded ivory launch plan rests on the tray rim at left, weighted by a graphite paperweight. Fine scuffs mark the hull, and dust sits in the wave grooves.
end: The same barge listing hard to the right. Its bow has dipped under the frosted acrylic waves, and the ivory product crate slides down the tilted deck, its wire snapped and one corner already in the water. Three of the four paper lifeboats have been cut loose from the budget and hang mid-fall from their davits, graphite lines coiling after them; the fourth dangles by one end. The acid-lime lifebuoy has jumped its clip and is caught in the air over the stern. Frosted spray lifts where the bow meets the waves. On the left, the launch plan has been swept off the tray rim and flutters open. Crumpled paper scraps drift on the surface, spreading outward from the hull.
apocalypse: A deep miniature sea floor of pale sediment stretches into dim, milky distance, lit from above through a ceiling of frosted acrylic waves. In the foreground lies the giant barge, broken in two across its middle, its graphite hull crusted with pale paper silt and its davits bent. The product crate has burst open on the seabed, its ivory card walls softened and collapsed. Three paper lifeboats lie scattered across the floor like pale husks. In the midground, a slim graphite salvage rig hangs from a vertical cable that rises out of frame, and its lime grab claw closes around one intact product carton, lifting it upward in a thin plume of silt toward a small graphite pontoon floating dark on the surface above.

title: Booby-trapped office
start: A small office corner sits on a pale neutral tabletop: a graphite doorframe about as tall as a coffee mug at left, a graphite desk in the midground and a tall graphite shelf at right. Across the foot of the doorway runs a single taut acid-lime tripwire, fixed to two tiny graphite eyelets. The wire's far end leads along the floor to a graphite stapler perched at the desk's edge. On the desk, a frosted acrylic pencil pot, a row of ivory binders and a roll of ivory tape sit in line, and a rolling graphite chair is parked nearby. The shelf holds a frosted glass jar of marbles and three stacked ivory boxes. Dust gathers along the skirting, and the binder spines show fine creases.
end: The same office mid-cascade, starting at the doorway. The acid-lime tripwire has been snagged and pulled tight, yanking the stapler off the desk edge; it hangs mid-drop and has knocked the pencil pot, which sprays pencils across the desktop. The pencils have struck the rolling chair, which is rolling right into the shelf. The shelf is tipping: the frosted marble jar has tumbled and is emptying, marbles bouncing across the floor, and the ivory boxes slide off in a stepped fall. Binders fan open as they topple like dominoes along the desk. The tape roll unspools across the floor. Dust rises in a line that follows the whole path back to the wire.
apocalypse: A long, narrow ravine winds through a wide ruin toward a pale horizon, its floor littered with oversized office traps long since sprung. Giant graphite shelves lie across it like fallen bridges, and frosted marbles the size of boulders sit where they rolled, filmed with dust. Toppled binders form a crooked ridge along one wall, their ivory covers split and bleached. A snapped graphite doorframe stands at the ravine's mouth, and old wires cross the floor at odd heights. In the midground, a slim six-legged graphite survey walker steps carefully along the ravine, planting small lime stakes on either side to mark one clear, safe path, while a flat graphite roller behind it presses the marked lane smooth and level.

title: Task board stampede
start: A flat game board of ivory card, about the size of a place mat, lies on a pale neutral tabletop, its surface ruled with a winding path of blank squares. Small task tiles of frosted acrylic, each the size of a sugar cube, sit stacked in a neat graphite tray at the board's left end. On the start square rests a single acid-lime token. Two blank-faced graphite dice sit in a frosted glass cup at the front right, waiting. Behind the board, a graphite desk holds a closed laptop and a pen holder, and a jacket hangs over its chair. Card fibres show along the board's folded hinge, and dust sits in the tray's corners.
end: The same board, erupting. The two graphite dice are caught mid-tumble across the board, and from the tray on the left a stampede of frosted task tiles pours out in a dense running wave, hundreds of them hopping and skidding along the path. The acid-lime token has been knocked off its start square and flung into the air. The wave has reached the desk behind: the pen holder is toppled with pens scattering, the laptop is shunted to the edge and tipping, and the chair is driven backward, its jacket flying. Tiles ricochet off the desk legs and skid off the table edge. Card dust and acrylic chips hang in the air, every trail pointing back to the tray.
apocalypse: A trampled plain stretches toward a hazy horizon, its ground churned into ruts and furrows packed with countless worn frosted tiles, chipped and milky, heaped into long ridges where the stampede passed. In the foreground, the giant ivory game board lies torn and curled up like a broken terrace, its path squares faded. The desk is flattened beneath a ridge of tiles, its laptop split open and bleached. A graphite die the size of a building sits embedded in a furrow. In the midground, a slim graphite sorting rig on long spider legs straddles the board, picking tiles from the ruts with a fine clamp and stacking them back in their tray, and its lime pointer arm sets one token squarely back on the start square.

title: Office chain reaction
start: A small desk fan with a brushed graphite cage and frosted acrylic blades, about the height of a mug, sits at the left of a pale neutral tabletop, aimed to the right. In front of it lies a loose stack of ivory paper, edges slightly misaligned. Next to the stack stands a full frosted mug, then a graphite power strip whose cord runs back to the fan. Beyond, a slim graphite wall shelf holding three ivory binders is mounted above a second desk in the right background. The fan's acid-lime power switch is just being clicked on, the only colour in the scene. The top sheet's corner curls up, and fine dust sits on the fan cage.
end: The same objects falling in sequence from left to right. The fan spins, its acid-lime switch on, and the top ivory sheet has lifted and flown into the frosted mug, tipping it. A sheet of grey coffee arcs out onto the graphite power strip, which gives a small pale spark and jerks its cord, yanking the shelf bracket loose. The shelf is caught mid-drop, its three ivory binders tumbling open, the first striking the second desk, which tips onto its side. Loose paper swirls in the fan's draught, droplets hang in the air, and dust and scraps trace a clear line from the last falling desk back to the fan.
apocalypse: A long valley stretches toward a hazy horizon, crossed by a line of giant toppled desks and shelves lying one against the next like fallen dominoes, each the size of a building, weathered, cracked and furred with pale dust. Drifts of ivory paper fill the gaps between them. At the near end, the enormous fan lies on its back, its frosted blades cracked. A colossal mug rests on its side, stained grey inside. The chain runs on down the valley, but in the midground the last desk still stands, leaning only slightly, held by a lime stop block that a slim graphite rail tractor has just pushed into place at its base, bracing it against the fall.

title: Frozen clock
start: A round office clock the width of a dinner plate stands on a brushed graphite easel at the back of a pale neutral tabletop. Its sandblasted frosted glass front covers a plain ivory dial with tick marks, and its slim graphite pointers rest a hair short of the top, the moment just before leaving time. A thin acid-lime second pointer is the only part expected to move. In front sits a small graphite desk with a chamfered top holding a neat stack of four ivory task cards squared to the edge and a closed graphite slab of a laptop. A jacket hangs over the chair back, ready to go, and a frosted acrylic desk lamp glows softly. A faint film of dust rests on the clock's machined rim.
end: The same clock and desk are held in a thin rime of frost, as if the room itself has stopped. The acid-lime second pointer is stuck mid-sweep just past the top tick, with fine ice crystals bridging it to the dial. Only the task pile has kept going: ivory cards rise from the desk in a leaning tower past the lamp, fresh cards hang mid-air as they drop onto it from above, and a slide of cards has spilled off the right edge, fanning across the floor and banking against the chair legs. The jacket has been dragged half off the chair by a card drift. Frost feathers creep across the frosted glass front, and frozen card fibres glitter across the desk.
apocalypse: A frost-bound plain of packed ivory card flakes, crusted and wind-scoured, stretches under a pale sky to a line of low ice ridges. Rising from it is the clock, now as tall as a water tower, tilted on its snapped graphite easel. Its frosted glass front is cracked in a wide star and packed with snow-like card fibre. The desk below has become a buried plateau, with only its chamfered corner and the lamp's frosted shade breaking the crust. Long drifts of frozen task cards run downwind from it in layered ridges. On the clock rim, a slim graphite climbing rig clamped to the bezel by four spidery legs has fitted a new lime second pointer to the hub, and the pointer has just moved one tick, shedding a thin curtain of frost.

title: Ticket rail overload
start: A short kitchen pass about a forearm wide sits on a pale neutral tabletop: a brushed graphite counter with chamfered edges and fine machining marks. Above it runs a slim graphite ticket rail on two brackets, and a frosted acrylic heat lamp hangs over the counter with a soft internal glow. One small ivory order slip is clipped to the rail by a single acid-lime rail clip, its blank front slightly curled at the bottom. On the counter below sits one ivory card plate, empty and clean. To the right, a stack of clean plates waits beside a folded apron. Faint grease-like smudges and paper lint mark the rail. Everything is orderly and ready for one order.
end: The same rail is overloaded. Order slips crowd along its whole length, overlapping three and four deep, bowing the rail in the middle, and fresh slips are frozen mid-fall as the clips give way. The acid-lime clip holding the first slip has been shoved to the far end and is sliding off. Dropped slips spill across the pass in a curling layer, and under the heat lamp the plates are now stacked high in leaning columns, one column tipping sideways toward the table edge with its top plate caught in the air. The apron is buried under slips. Curled paper edges browned by the lamp's heat and a haze of lint trace the overflow back to the rail.
apocalypse: A wide white drift field of old order slips, compacted and curled like wind-packed snow, rolls away toward a low horizon. Rising from it is the ruin of the kitchen pass, now the length of a street: the graphite counter cracked and tilted, the heat lamp's frosted shade split and half filled with slips, and plate columns standing as leaning, weathered towers. The ticket rail lies sagging across the drifts on its broken brackets. In the foreground, a slim graphite rail-crawler has re-hung a clean straight section of rail on new supports. Its jointed arm lifts slips from the drift one at a time, and a row of lime clips holds them in a neat ordered line along the repaired section.

title: Paperwork twister
start: A small graphite desk with a chamfered top sits on a pale neutral tabletop beside an open window frame of brushed graphite fitted with a tilted sandblasted frosted glass pane. On the desk lies a neat stack of ivory forms squared to the edge, and on top of it one loose form lifts slightly at its acid-lime corner tab, just caught by a draught. A graphite paperweight sits next to the stack, not on it. To the right, a frosted acrylic in-tray holds more forms, and a jacket hangs over the chair. Fine fibres rise from the lifted corner. The rest of the room is still and orderly.
end: The draught has become a storm through the same window. The loose form with its acid-lime tab is at the top of a spiralling column of paperwork that rises from the desk to the ceiling: sheets from the stack and the in-tray are caught mid-whirl, twisting in a tight funnel, with a trail of forms feeding into its base from the scattered stack. The in-tray has flipped and is airborne, the paperweight has slid to the desk edge, and the chair has rolled back with the jacket flapping off it. The frosted glass pane has swung wide open. Dust and paper fibres swirl around the column, and the whole spiral leans back toward the window.
apocalypse: A vast flattened plain stretches to a low horizon under a clearing sky, its surface combed into long curved streaks of pale forms laid down by the storm, some pressed flat, some curled into ridges. Near the centre, the desk lies overturned at the scale of a bridge, graphite legs pointing up, and the window frame stands alone, cracked and leaning, its frosted pane shattered. Torn forms have piled against it in a tall drift. In the middle distance, a slim graphite collector rig on thin wheels moves across the plain, a lime anemometer spinning calmly on its mast, while its low scoop feeds forms onto a neat squared stack on its back.
